scenes.tts: How can one missed separation give one gamete extra chromosome material and another too little? Watch one replicated chromosome pair cross both meiotic divisions.
scenes.caption: How can one missed separation give one gamete extra chromosome material and another too little? Watch one replicated chromosome pair cross both meiotic divisions.
scenes.visual: Hook first. Fill the frame with one cell and a large replicated chromosome pair: one blue homologue and one gold homologue, each drawn as two joined rods. A grey spindle tugs both homologues toward the same pole, while four empty gamete circles wait below. Put the question above the cell. Keep every chromosome gently vibrating under spindle tension. Colour map for both films: blue = one homologue, gold = the other homologue, teal = moved chromosome segment, green = balanced dose, red = extra or missing dose, grey = spindle and cell structure.
scenes.narration: How can one missed separation give one gamete extra chromosome material and another too little? Watch one replicated chromosome pair cross both meiotic divisions.

scenes.visual: Title card after the hook: When Chromosomes Miss Their Turn. Reuse the large blue and gold chromosome pair behind the title at low opacity.

scenes.tts: Each homologue has joined sister chromatids. Blue marks one homologue, and gold marks the other. The centromeres remain visible as small circles. At meiosis one, homologues normally move apart. At meiosis two, sisters normally separate. The first division sorts homologues; the second sorts copies within each homologue.
scenes.caption: Each homologue has joined sister chromatids. Blue marks one homologue, and gold marks the other. The centromeres remain visible as small circles. At meiosis I, homologues normally move apart. At meiosis II, sisters normally separate. The first division sorts homologues; the second sorts copies within each homologue.
scenes.visual: Return to the cell. First highlight the blue and gold homologues as whole X-shaped objects. Then pulse both rods within each X to identify sisters. Animate the first cell division horizontally, keeping sister rods joined. Animate the second division vertically, separating sister rods into four fixed gamete circles. Labels appear only when named: homologues, sisters, centromere, meiosis I, meiosis II.
scenes.narration: Each homologue has joined sister chromatids. Blue marks one homologue, and gold marks the other. The centromeres remain visible as small circles. At meiosis I, homologues normally move apart. At meiosis II, sisters normally separate. The first division sorts homologues; the second sorts copies within each homologue.

scenes.tts: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to part during a division. The resulting gamete may carry an extra chromosome or none of that chromosome. This is aneuploidy, a gain or loss of individual chromosomes rather than a whole set.
scenes.caption: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to part during a division. The resulting gamete may carry an extra chromosome or none of that chromosome. This is aneuploidy, a gain or loss of individual chromosomes rather than a whole set.
scenes.visual: Rewind the normal animation to one cell. Freeze the grey spindle while blue and gold remain together, then release both toward one pole. A vertical schematic dose gauge appears at the edge, centred on green NORMAL, with red EXTRA above and red MISSING below. Mark the picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Nondisjunction means chromosomes fail to part during a division. The resulting gamete may carry an extra chromosome or none of that chromosome. This is aneuploidy, a gain or loss of individual chromosomes rather than a whole set.

scenes.tts: First, let both homologues travel together at meiosis one. One daughter cell receives blue and gold. The other receives neither. Their sister chromatids remain joined, so the first division has already created a dose imbalance.
scenes.caption: First, let both homologues travel together at meiosis I. One daughter cell receives blue and gold. The other receives neither. Their sister chromatids remain joined, so the first division has already created a dose imbalance.
scenes.visual: Show the meiosis I error at large scale. Both X-shaped homologues glide into the upper daughter cell; the lower daughter cell stays empty. The dose gauge splits into two copies: upper points to EXTRA and lower points to MISSING. Keep the four final gamete circles empty so the outcome is not revealed yet.
scenes.narration: First, let both homologues travel together at meiosis I. One daughter cell receives blue and gold. The other receives neither. Their sister chromatids remain joined, so the first division has already created a dose imbalance.

scenes.tts: Now suppose meiosis two runs normally. Can separating the sisters repair the chromosome dose, or is the final pattern already fixed?
scenes.caption: Now suppose meiosis II runs normally. Can separating the sisters repair the chromosome dose, or is the final pattern already fixed?
scenes.visual: Hold both daughter cells above four empty gamete circles. Add two possible arrows: a teal question-mark arrow labelled REPAIR? and a red arrow labelled IMBALANCE REMAINS? Keep slow spindle motion but do not move any chromosome into a gamete.
scenes.narration: Now suppose meiosis II runs normally. Can separating the sisters repair the chromosome dose, or is the final pattern already fixed?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the question visible and the spindles moving subtly. Do not reveal either answer.

scenes.tts: The later division cannot replace a missing homologue. Normal sister separation produces matching outcomes within each branch. The products from one branch carry both homologues. The products from the other carry neither. The counts appear on screen.
scenes.caption: The later division cannot replace a missing homologue. Normal sister separation produces matching outcomes within each branch. The products from one branch carry both homologues. The products from the other carry neither. The counts appear on screen.
scenes.visual: Remove the REPAIR arrow. Complete meiosis II. The upper branch sends one blue rod and one gold rod into each of two gametes; the lower branch makes two empty gametes. On screen only, label the four bins '2 disomic' and '2 nullisomic'. Pulse both red dose states.
scenes.narration: The later division cannot replace a missing homologue. Normal sister separation produces matching outcomes within each branch. The products from one branch carry both homologues. The products from the other carry neither. The counts appear on screen.

scenes.tts: Reset to normal meiosis one. Blue and gold separate into different daughter cells. During meiosis two, blue sisters fail to part in only one cell. Gold sisters still separate normally in the other cell.
scenes.caption: Reset to normal meiosis I. Blue and gold separate into different daughter cells. During meiosis II, blue sisters fail to part in only one cell. Gold sisters still separate normally in the other cell.
scenes.visual: Transform the finished meiosis I diagram into a normal split, blue above and gold below. In the blue daughter, both blue sister rods move together into one gamete while its partner stays empty. In the gold daughter, one gold rod enters each gamete. Keep all four gamete positions identical to the previous scene.
scenes.narration: Reset to normal meiosis I. Blue and gold separate into different daughter cells. During meiosis II, blue sisters fail to part in only one cell. Gold sisters still separate normally in the other cell.

scenes.tts: This error makes three dose classes instead of two. One product has extra material, one is missing it, and the remaining products are normal. The stage of the missed separation sets the product pattern. It also leaves a fingerprint that DNA markers in the child can read.
scenes.caption: This error makes three dose classes instead of two. One product has extra material, one is missing it, and the remaining products are normal. The stage of the missed separation sets the product pattern. It also leaves a fingerprint that DNA markers in the child can read.
scenes.visual: Align the meiosis I outcome above the meiosis II outcome. Use identical four-bin rows. On screen, show 'MI: 2 extra | 2 missing' and 'MII: 1 extra | 1 missing | 2 normal'. Numbers remain visual only. Sweep a bracket from the failed division to its product row. Do not show markers or alleles; the text works out the fingerprint.
scenes.narration: This error makes three dose classes instead of two. One product has extra material, one is missing it, and the remaining products are normal. The stage of the missed separation sets the product pattern. It also leaves a fingerprint that DNA markers in the child can read.

scenes.tts: A normal gamete contributes one copy at fertilization. A gamete with extra material can therefore make a trisomic zygote. A gamete missing that chromosome can make a monosomic zygote. That starting dose is copied as the zygote divides.
scenes.caption: A normal gamete contributes one copy at fertilization. A gamete with extra material can therefore make a trisomic zygote. A gamete missing that chromosome can make a monosomic zygote. That starting dose is copied as the zygote divides.
scenes.visual: Move a grey normal egg chromosome into one disomic gamete, forming a zygote with blue, gold and grey rods. Separately, move a grey chromosome into a nullisomic gamete, forming a one-rod zygote. On screen label them 'trisomy' and 'monosomy'. Each zygote divides once while retaining its chromosome count.
scenes.narration: A normal gamete contributes one copy at fertilization. A gamete with extra material can therefore make a trisomic zygote. A gamete missing that chromosome can make a monosomic zygote. That starting dose is copied as the zygote divides.

scenes.tts: Extra or missing chromosome material changes the copies of many genes together. That can alter development and survival. Most aneuploid human embryos do not survive pregnancy. Trisomy twenty-one is among the few autosomal trisomies seen regularly at birth.
scenes.caption: Extra or missing chromosome material changes the copies of many genes together. That can alter development and survival. Most aneuploid human embryos do not survive pregnancy. Trisomy 21 is among the few autosomal trisomies seen regularly at birth.
scenes.visual: Zoom into labelled gene blocks along the three zygote chromosomes. Each block appears three times, then the dose gauge rises to EXTRA. Transform to a restrained human-development timeline marked 'outcomes vary'; fade most schematic paths before birth without labels such as rejected or extinct. Keep one trisomy 21 path visible and labelled.
scenes.narration: Extra or missing chromosome material changes the copies of many genes together. That can alter development and survival. Most aneuploid human embryos do not survive pregnancy. Trisomy 21 is among the few autosomal trisomies seen regularly at birth.

scenes.tts: The division error explains the product pattern. DNA dose explains why the pattern matters biologically. Keep those questions separate: where did separation fail, and what chromosome material became extra or missing? The same count can hide different routes to imbalance.
scenes.caption: The division error explains the product pattern. DNA dose explains why the pattern matters biologically. Keep those questions separate: where did separation fail, and what chromosome material became extra or missing? The same count can hide different routes to imbalance.
scenes.visual: Return to the carried four-bin layout. A grey arrow points from the failed division to PRODUCT PATTERN. A second arrow points from red dose gauges to BIOLOGICAL CONSEQUENCES. End with both arrows surrounding the blue and gold chromosome pair.
scenes.narration: The division error explains the product pattern. DNA dose explains why the pattern matters biologically. Keep those questions separate: where did separation fail, and what chromosome material became extra or missing? The same count can hide different routes to imbalance.

scenes.visual: One-line end card only: 'Chromosome-number changes matter through DNA dose.'
